Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma, the combination of threat items is not fully coherent: startle response and physical reactivity fit PTSD, but risky behavior is a different symptom style and is weakly connected to the rest of this profile. With only Threat and Memory represented, risky behavior lacks support from the other selected items and does not read as a clear trauma-linked threat perception.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: Within Memory, the items suggest overwhelmed, poorly verbalized traumatic recall, which is coherent for PTSD. However, intense guilt on recall introduces a strong negative appraisal theme that is otherwise absent from the profile. Given the formulation only shows a Threat → Memory link and no active Negative Appraisals connections, this item is not well aligned with the stated cognitive pattern.

vignette:
Kofi Mensah is a 46-year-old African American man who works as a curriculum designer for a mid-sized urban school district. He is married, describes his relationship as generally supportive, and came to the initial intake presenting with a PCL-5 score of 69 - a level of symptom severity that his wife had, by his account, been urging him to address for months before he finally agreed to make the call.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Kofi was driving home from a late evening at the district office when he was pulled over on a highway interchange he uses almost every workday. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated rapidly. Within seconds of rolling down his window, he found himself facing drawn weapons, shouted commands that contradicted one another, and officers who, he felt certain, were not seeing a curriculum designer returning from work - they were seeing something else entirely. He was ordered out of the vehicle, forced to the ground, and held at gunpoint for what he later learned was nearly twenty minutes before a supervisor arrived and the situation was stood down. No charges were filed. No explanation was given. He drove the rest of the way home in silence, hands trembling on the wheel, and did not speak about it for three weeks.

In the months that followed, Kofi's body began registering danger before his mind had time to catch up. The hypervigilance that settled into his daily life was not abstract; it was architectural. He began scanning every room he entered, noting exits, watching hands. At the district office, where he spends most of his working hours moving between open-plan spaces and conference rooms, he repositioned himself habitually so that no one could approach him from behind. The sound of a door opening sharply, a colleague raising their voice down the hall, a phone buzzing unexpectedly on a hard surface - any of these could produce a startle response so pronounced that coworkers had begun to notice and comment. When something in the environment reminded him of the stop - the flash of blue and red light from a passing emergency vehicle visible through the office windows, the crackle of a radio, even the particular quality of highway noise that drifted in during evening meetings - his body flooded with physical reactivity: his chest tightened, his breathing became shallow, his hands went cold. These moments of heightened alertness and physical alarm did not resolve cleanly. Instead, they opened a door.

What came through that door was not, in any straightforward sense, a memory. This is what Kofi found most disorienting and most difficult to describe during intake. When the threat response was activated - when his body was already on high alert - something returned that he could not quite name. He had come to believe that the event had simply not lodged in his mind the way other memories did, because he could not seem to put it into words. When he tried to recall what had happened on that interchange, he hit a wall of emotion so overwhelming that he had to stop - mid-sentence in session, mid-thought at his desk. What arrived was not an image, not a sequence, not a narrative he could follow to its end. It was feeling without picture: the absolute certainty of imminent harm, the specific quality of powerlessness, the cold of the pavement - present in his body, untethered from any clear scene. The state of alarm that his hypervigilance and physical reactivity produced seemed to call this emotional residue forward, so that the threat he was monitoring for in the present collapsed into the threat he had not yet fully processed from the past.

By the time Kofi sought help, he had quietly stopped taking the highway interchange on his commute, adding twenty-five minutes to a journey he makes five days a week. He had not told his employer why his productivity had dipped, and he had not told his wife the full account of what happened that night. What finally brought him in was a moment at work when a colleague touched his shoulder from behind and he reacted so sharply that he frightened her. He was most afraid, he said, that he would never be able to simply remember what had happened - that it would always arrive this way, as sensation without story, as a feeling his body knew and his mind could not hold.
